title: Write it again (Jeremiah 36)
hook: the king burns the scroll column by column, and Jeremiah dictates it again
carry: there were added besides unto them many like words

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah paid silver for a field in a city about to fall, and sealed the deed in a jar. Your line was plant the tree, sign the lease. Did you make a small down payment on a hope? Today, the words themselves go into the fire. Day eight hundred eight.

A penknife. A brazier of coals. A long roll of writing. It's winter, and King Jehoiakim is sitting in his winter house with a fire burning on the hearth in front of him. A man named Jehudi is reading aloud to him from a scroll: every warning Jeremiah has spoken, written down by the scribe Baruch. And every time Jehudi finishes three or four columns, the king reaches over, cuts that piece off with the penknife, and drops it into the fire. Then he waits for the next part. He listens to the whole thing, piece by piece, until the entire scroll is ash.
screen: `A WINTER HOUSE, A FIRE.` → `THREE OR FOUR COLUMNS AT A TIME.` → `THE WHOLE SCROLL IS ASH.`

segments.voice: Back up a little. Jeremiah is barred from going to the Temple, so he dictates his words, and Baruch writes them in a roll. Baruch then reads it aloud in the Lord's house, on a fast day, where the people can hear. Some officials hear it and are shaken. They tell Baruch: go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are. Then they tell the king, and he sends for the scroll. Now notice who is in the room. The text says that the king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and did not tear their garments. But a few officials, named in the text, Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, begged the king not to burn the scroll. He would not listen. So the fire wins. Or seems to. Then comes a short instruction, in the King James words: "Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll." And Jeremiah does. He dictates, and Baruch writes, all over again. And the chapter ends with a quiet detail: there were added besides unto them many like words. The second scroll is longer than the first. That's what this chapter seems to hand down: a king can burn a page, but he can't burn the person who remembers it, or the friend holding the pen. Jewish custom treats a worn-out Torah scroll with care, burying it rather than throwing it away, and new scrolls are written by hand, letter by letter. The answer to the knife and the fire is a scribe, a fresh roll, and patience.
screen: `BARUCH READS IN THE TEMPLE.` · `SOME BEG THE KING TO STOP.` · then, large: `TAKE THEE AGAIN ANOTHER ROLL.` · then: `THE SECOND SCROLL IS LONGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rewrite something that was lost. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that slipped away. A recipe from someone who's gone. A story your grandfather told. A note you deleted. A plan that burned down. Let your mind go back and gather what it can, one piece at a time, the way Jeremiah spoke and Baruch wrote. Don't worry about getting it exact. Just notice which pieces are still there. If something new arrives that wasn't in the first version, let it in too. If you pray, you can ask for help remembering. The bell holds the time.
Baruch, the scribe who wrote Jeremiah's words on a scroll, and wrote them all again after the king burned it. Today's word.
Your line: there were added besides unto them many like words. Today, put on paper one thing you found in the sit, even a few lines of it, before it slips away a second time. Day eight hundred eight.

howItsDone: Jews read Jeremiah 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the scene of Baruch writing at Jeremiah's dictation is often taught alongside the care Jewish tradition gives to handwritten scrolls.

go to the palace and argue.

original.note: Hebrew: scroll, a roll of writing; the King James calls it a roll.

trapdoor: what you thought: the king burned the prophet's words, so they were gone.
what it means: Jeremiah and Baruch wrote them again, and added more.
what a scholar hears: the chapter shows how prophecy was dictated, written, read aloud and rewritten, a look at a book being made.

sources.quoted: Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll.

notes: 'Three or four columns' follows Jeremiah 36:23 (KJV 'three or four leaves'; Hebrew delatot, columns).
The Temple reading on a fast day follows Jeremiah 36:6, 9.
The line about burying an unusable Torah scroll (genizah) is a practice statement, not from Jeremiah 36; Keeper may wish to confirm wording or cut.
Quotation is KJV; Keeper may prefer JPS 1917.
Editor: the officials tell the king and he sends for the scroll (36:20–21), rather than carrying it in themselves; cut 'rare' from the trapdoor.
Audit: cut the filler line 'Losing words is not the end of them.' The Hebrew of 36:23 is ambiguous whether the king or Jehudi does the cutting; the script follows the reading that the king cuts.
